correction.text: Slovakia without the southern strip awarded to Hungary at Vienna on 2 November 1938 (the 11,833 km2 of the south that the Slovak–Hungarian War page names)

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe, Cliopatria has none for Slovakia 1939-1945 (its Czechoslovakia row jumps from 1938 to 1947). The shape is the state of 14 March 1939: Slovakia without the south awarded to Hungary at Vienna. Resolved with tools/gazetteer.py it is 136 cells (about 34,400 km2; infobox area 38,055 km2 for 1939, ratio 0.90, fine). It still holds the eastern Stakčín–Sobrance strip (the cells at Sobrance and Stakčín are inside it) and does not yet hold Polish Orava and Spiš (Jabłonka and Niedzica are outside it, because {country: Slovakia} is the modern state). The ledger moves both: the 4 April 1939 loss takes the strip (1,697 km2) out for Hungary and the 21 November 1939 gain adds Orava and Spiš (752 km2) from Poland. From 29 August 1944 the German occupation and the insurgent zone overlay this shape, and from 19 January 1945 the Red Army's contest zone in the east (ledger).

region.text: Slovakia without the southern strip awarded to Hungary at Vienna on 2 November 1938 (the 11,833 km2 of the south that the Slovak–Hungarian War page names)

ledger.note: 14 March 1939: the Slovak Diet declares an independent Slovak State, a client of Nazi Germany. 'Parliament unanimously voted to secede from Czecho-Slovakia'; infobox 'existed between 14 March 1939 and 4 April 1945'; Hitler 'urged him to proclaim Slovakia's independence'.

region.text: Slovakia without the southern strip awarded to Hungary at Vienna on 2 November 1938 (the 11,833 km2 of the south that the Slovak–Hungarian War page names)

ledger.note: 23 March 1939: the Treaty of Protection makes the new state a German client. The page: the treaty, 'signed on 23 March 1939, partially subordinated its foreign, military, and economic policy to that of Germany'; the Wehrmacht set up the 'Protective Zone' (Schutzzone) in western Slovakia in August 1939. The nazi-germany dossier carries the mirror (vassal_start 1939-3, counterpart slovak-republic).

region.text: a strip of eastern Slovak territory (1,697 km2, 69,930 inhabitants, 78 municipalities) around the towns of Stakčín and Sobrance

ledger.note: 23 March 1939: Hungary attacks eastern Slovakia. The Slovak–Hungarian War 'was a war fought from 23 March to 31 March 1939 between the First Slovak Republic and Hungary in eastern Slovakia'; the Slovak Republic page gives 23-31 March.

region.text: a strip of eastern Slovak territory (1,697 km2, 69,930 inhabitants, 78 municipalities) around the towns of Stakčín and Sobrance

ledger.note: 4 April 1939: the war ends in the Budapest treaty. A German-brokered ceasefire came about 25 March, fighting ended 31 March, and 'by a treaty signed on 4 April in Budapest' the strip was ceded.

region.text: a strip of eastern Slovak territory (1,697 km2, 69,930 inhabitants, 78 municipalities) around the towns of Stakčín and Sobrance

ledger.note: 4 April 1939: Slovakia cedes the Stakčín–Sobrance strip to Hungary. 'forced to cede to Hungary a strip of eastern Slovak territory (1,697 km2, 69,930 inhabitants, 78 municipalities)', 'corresponding today to the area around the towns of Stakčín and Sobrance'; the Slovak Republic page says 'cede 1,697 square kilometres'. Hungary kept it until 1945.

region.text: the areas of Orava and Spiš, 752 km2 with 30,000 people

ledger.note: 21 November 1939: Germany hands Slovakia Orava and Spiš, taken from Poland. 'Following Slovak participation in the invasion of Poland in September 1939, border adjustments increased the Slovak Republic's geographical extent in the areas of Orava and Spiš', 'on the basis of an agreement (November 21, 1939) between Germany and Slovakia', 'a total of 752 square kilometers of land with 30,000 people'. The land was Polish since 1920/1924; Germany, which had conquered it, disposed of it.

region.text: the insurgents' territory, about 22,000 km2 at first, centred on Banská Bystrica and the Zvolen–Brezno triangle

ledger.note: 29 August 1944: the Slovak National Uprising begins at Banská Bystrica against the Tiso government and the German troops. 'In the first days of the uprising, the insurgents' territory covered about 22,000 km²'; by the end of September the territory 'had been reduced to 6,800 km²'. The insurgents (Slovak National Council, rebel army) are not a state that held land for a year, so there is no rebel dossier.

29 August 1944: Germany occupies Slovakia. 'the German invasion of Slovakia by the Wehrmacht, which began on 29 August 1944'; the Slovak Republic page: 'the Republic lost independence to a complete German occupation'. The page dates the occupation to the days after the Martin incident of 27 August, not to a single day.

region.text: the insurgents' territory, reduced to under 7,000 km2 by early October

ledger.note: 28 October 1944: organised insurgent resistance collapses. Banská Bystrica 'was captured by Kampfgruppe Schill on 27 October' and on the night of 28 October General Viest 'accepted the defeat of the insurgent army as an organised unit'. Guerrilla fighting went on in the hills.

region.text: eastern Slovakia, the Prešov and Košice regions without the south that Hungary held since the Vienna Award (Košice city itself was in that south); the page names Bardejov, Svidník, Prešov and Košice as taken on 19 January 1945

ledger.note: 19 January 1945: the Red Army enters eastern Slovakia. 'On January 19, 1945, the Red Army occupied Bardejov, Svidník, Prešov and Košice in eastern Slovakia'; the Western Carpathian offensive page: it 'lasted from January 12 to February 18, 1945', 'the next day Prešov was captured by Soviet troops' (19 January), and the 2nd Ukrainian Front 'continued the fighting until mid-March and reached the Hron River'. The eastern third of the state is thus no longer under Bratislava or the Wehrmacht before Bratislava falls; the front further west (Banská Bystrica liberated 26 March) is not drawn, the pages give no other dated lines.

region.text: Slovakia, from which the Wehrmacht was driven by the Red Army

ledger.note: April 1945: the Red Army drives the Germans out. 'captured Bratislava during the Bratislava–Brno offensive and occupied all of Slovakia'; 'until the Red Army liberated Slovakia from Nazi control in April 1945'.

region.text: eastern Slovakia, the Prešov and Košice regions without the south that Hungary held since the Vienna Award (Košice city itself was in that south); the page names Bardejov, Svidník, Prešov and Košice as taken on 19 January 1945

ledger.note: 4 April 1945: Bratislava falls to the 2nd Ukrainian Front in the Bratislava–Brno offensive and the Red Army 'occupied all of Slovakia'; the fighting on Slovak soil ends with the state. The east had been held by the Red Army since January and February; there is no dated end of the fighting there, so the contest runs to the fall of the capital.

region.text: Slovakia without the southern strip awarded to Hungary at Vienna on 2 November 1938 (the 11,833 km2 of the south that the Slovak–Hungarian War page names)

ledger.note: 4 April 1945: the client state ends with the fall of Bratislava (infobox 'Fall of Bratislava: 4 April 1945'); the exiled government capitulated on 8 May 1945. From 29 August 1944 the German occupation (occupation_start above) overlays the client relation: the page says the 'Republic lost independence to a complete German occupation', yet Tiso stayed in office. The nazi-germany dossier closes its vassal_end in May 1945 (German-occupied Europe table), one month later.

region.text: the Slovak State, 'reintegrated into the recreated Third Czechoslovak Republic'

ledger.note: 4 April 1945: the Slovak Republic ends with the fall of Bratislava; its territory 'was reintegrated into the recreated Third Czechoslovak Republic'. The exiled Slovak government 'capitulated to General Walton Walker' on 8 May 1945.

wars.name: Slovak–Hungarian War

zones.text: a strip of eastern Slovak territory (1,697 km2, 69,930 inhabitants, 78 municipalities) around the towns of Stakčín and Sobrance

wars.outcome: Hungary wins a strip of eastern Slovakia (1,697 km2) by the Budapest treaty of 4 April 1939; a ceasefire came about 25 March and fighting stopped 31 March.
wars.note: The Slovak Republic page counts the 'border war' from 23 to 31 March. The 2 November 1938 First Vienna Award (11,833 km2 of south Slovakia) is a separate, earlier loss, recorded in the czechoslovakia dossier.

wars.name: Invasion of Poland
wars.outcome: Slovakia took part with Germany in September 1939 and was awarded Orava and Spiš by the German–Slovak agreement of 21 November 1939.
wars.note: The Invasion of Poland article itself was not opened (page budget); the Slovak Republic page gives the participation and the award.

wars.name: Slovak National Uprising

zones.text: the insurgents' territory in central Slovakia

wars.outcome: The German troops and Slovak loyalists crush the organised uprising: Banská Bystrica falls 27 October and Viest's last order is given 28 October 1944; insurgent territory fell from about 22,000 km2 to under 7,000 km2.
wars.note: Wehrmacht troops had entered Slovakia from 29 August 1944; the Slovak State stayed a German-occupied client until the Red Army took Bratislava on 4 April 1945.

wars.name: Western Carpathian offensive

zones.text: eastern Slovakia, the Prešov and Košice regions without the south that Hungary held since the Vienna Award (Košice city itself was in that south); the page names Bardejov, Svidník, Prešov and Košice as taken on 19 January 1945

wars.outcome: The Red Army takes eastern Slovakia from 19 January 1945 (Prešov the same day); the Western Carpathian offensive 'lasted from January 12 to February 18, 1945', the 2nd Ukrainian Front reached the Hron by mid-March and took Bratislava on 4 April 1945, ending the Slovak State.
wars.note: The offensive page does not give the front on 18 February and does not mention the Bratislava–Brno offensive; the later dates (Banská Bystrica 26 March, Bratislava 4 April) are from the Slovak Republic page. The Slovak army is not named as a combatant on the Axis side by either page; the state is listed because the land was its own.

certainty.note: Borders follow treaties: the 2 November 1938 Vienna Award line, the 4 April 1939 Budapest treaty and the 21 November 1939 German–Slovak agreement. The insurgent zone of autumn 1944 is soft (its extent is given in km2 only).

notes: Client state of Nazi Germany. The Treaty of Protection of 23 March 1939 (the page: 'signed on 23 March 1939'; the Slovak–Hungarian War page cites 18 March for a guarantee treaty) and the German 'Protective Zone' in western Slovakia from August 1939 are the Axis relation, recorded here as vassal_start (1939-3) and vassal_end (1945-4) with nazi-germany and mirrored in the nazi-germany dossier (vassal_start 1939-3, vassal_end 1945-5). The Slovak Republic page does not date the Slovak invasion of Poland beyond 'September 1939'. Prime ministers (Tuka, Štefan Tiso) were not read, so only the president is listed in rulers. Region names the gazetteer lacks: Orava, Spiš (regions), Sobrance (place). The 1939 shape is the state of 14 March 1939: it still holds the Stakčín–Sobrance strip until the 4 April 1939 loss event and does not hold Polish Orava and Spiš until the 21 November 1939 gain event. The Red Army's advance of 1945 is one contest zone for the east (19 January to 4 April 1945, counterpart union-of-soviet-socialist-republics); the western front lines (Hron by mid-March, Banská Bystrica 26 March) are not drawn. The page gives no year for the 2,655,053 population estimate.
